title: Gardner's Witchcraft Today: Modern Wicca Founded on Murray's Thesis
description: Gerald Gardner published Witchcraft Today in 1954, presenting himself as an initiate of a surviving coven of pre-Christian witches and drawing explicitly on Margaret Murray's discredited historical thesis to provide legitimacy for modern Wicca. Gardner claimed that contemporary practitioners preserved an ancient fertility religion that Murray had identified in the historical witch trials. In fact, Wicca was largely Gardner's own creation, drawing on Aleister Crowley's occultism, Freemasonry, ceremonial magic, and Murray's fabricated history. Gardner's foundation of modern Wicca created a persistent popular conflation between the historical witch prosecutions and contemporary neo-pagan religious practice — a conflation that historians of the early modern period have spent decades trying to disentangle.
historiographical_note: Ronald Hutton's The Triumph of the Moon: A History of Modern Pagan Witchcraft (1999) is the definitive scholarly account of Wicca's origins, documenting Gardner's eclecticism and the absence of continuous tradition from the early modern period. Hutton's work is sensitive to Wicca as a genuine modern religious movement while firmly distinguishing it from any historical continuity with early modern witch prosecution. The Gardner-Murray connection illustrates how historical scholarship (even bad scholarship) can shape religious movements.
source_method: Gardner, Witchcraft Today (1954); Hutton, The Triumph of the Moon (1999); secondary scholarship on modern Paganism
